Prevention: Hang yellow thick polythene sheets pasted with gel/sticky surface about five feet by two feet close to the crops.
Avoid inter planting citrus with beans, grape, guava, chillies, peppers, mango, pomegranate, pineapple which are susceptible to attack by the moth.
Monitoring: Look for a discoloured entry point on premature ripened and fallen fruits.
Look for larvae with yellowish-white with dark spots and a yellow-brown head.
The young larvae mines fruit surfaces or bore the skin causing premature ripening of the fruit.
Adult moths have grey, brown, black forewings with orange-brown markings.
False codling has a triangular marking near the edges of the wings.
Dissect the fruits and look for larva or fruit rot due to feeding which may also lead to fungal infections.
Take action when 10 or more moths are seen per trap per week.
Direct Control: Increase the pheromone traps density to 2 traps per hectare to control the pest.

Use mesh or net barriers to keep the pest out of the crop or hand pick the mature larvae from the crop.
Biologics at two traps per hectare with action thresholds of 5-7 moths caught per hectare per night.
Bacillus thuringiensis at 0.49kg/acre to effective manage this pest.

Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance
Always consult the most recent list of registered pesticides (PCPB)
